steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An income statement (profit and loss account) shows revenue, costs, and profit over a period: revenue - cost of sales = gross profit; gross profit - expenses = net profit.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A balance sheet shows what a business OWNS (assets) and OWES (liabilities) at a specific date: assets = liabilities + capital. It's a snapshot of financial position.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Gross profit margin = (gross profit / revenue) x 100. It shows how efficiently the business produces its goods - a higher margin means lower production costs relative to selling price.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Net profit margin = (net profit / revenue) x 100. It shows overall profitability after ALL costs - a higher margin means better overall cost control.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Calculate the gross profit margin and net profit margin for a business with revenue £200,000, cost of sales £120,000, and expenses £50,000. | Explain what a current ratio of 0.8 means for a business and suggest what it should do. | Evaluate why financial ratios are useful but also have limitations when comparing business performance.

steps.title: Check your answers

Net profit margin = (£30,000 / £200,000) x 100 = 15%. steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always show the FORMULA first, then substitute, then calculate - this gets method marks even if arithmetic is wrong. When comparing ratios, specify the DIRECTION: 'the gross profit margin has increased from 35% to 40%, meaning...' A current ratio below 1 is a red flag, but a very high current ratio (>3) is also problematic - it means money is sitting idle.
